entities.summary:
Simon de Cramaud (d. 1423), a pivotal figure in late medieval ecclesiastical politics, served as a prominent French prelate and jurist whose career was inextricably linked to the profound institutional crisis of the Great Western Schism (1378–1417). Holding successive bishoprics in France—including Poitiers (1385), Carcassonne (1391), and Montpellier (1409)—and eventually attaining the titular Latin Patriarchate of Alexandria (1391) and the cardinalate (1413), Cramaud emerged as a leading proponent of conciliarism. His intellectual and diplomatic efforts were central to attempts at resolving the schism by asserting the authority of a general council over competing papal claims, fundamentally challenging the established papal monarchy and shaping the future of church governance.

Cramaud's influence solidified through his instrumental role in various councils and diplomatic initiatives aimed at ending the schism. He presided over the pivotal Council of Pisa in 1409, which attempted to depose both Pope Gregory XII (Roman Obedience) and Antipope Benedict XIII (Avignon Obedience) and elect a new pope, Alexander V. Although Pisa ultimately exacerbated the schism by creating a third claimant, Cramaud's legal and theological arguments at the council, particularly his advocacy for the 'via concilii' (the way of the council), provided a crucial intellectual framework for subsequent efforts. He also played a significant part in the French withdrawal of obedience from Benedict XIII, contributing to the growing pressure on the Avignon papacy.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Simon of Cramaud was a leading intellectual and political force in the conciliar movement, which fundamentally challenged papal authority during the Great Western Schism. His actions and arguments at the Council of Pisa laid critical groundwork for the eventual resolution of the schism at the Council of Constance, significantly shaping the future of church governance.
